summary: Learners aged 12–13 construct and interpret ray diagrams for plane mirrors and converging (convex) lenses, then classify the resulting image as real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished, and tie each case to a real device (camera, projector, magnifying glass). The spine is predict–observe–reconcile: pupils predict a striking outcome, observe it with real apparatus or a manipulable model, then reconcile it with a ray diagram so the diagram feels necessary rather than decorative. The load-bearing idea is that every point on an object radiates light in all directions and a ray diagram simply picks two convenient rays to locate one image point. Ray diagrams demand formal, counterfactual reasoning and are documented as resistant even in college, so at this age this is demanding threshold work; watch for rote-without-transfer.
misconceptions: Rote-without-transfer: pupils recite 'the image is the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front' but cannot use a diagram to answer a real question, e.g. whether stepping back changes how much of themselves they see — the signature Goldberg & McDermott finding.

'Cover half the lens → get half the image' (and 'each part of the lens makes its own bit of the picture') — in fact the WHOLE image remains, just dimmer, because every part of the lens forms the whole image.
'Remove the lens → the image stays on the screen (maybe blurry), or becomes upright' — in fact the image disappears entirely; the lens is what makes the rays converge.

Line-of-sight misconception: an image can be seen only if it lies along the straight line of sight to the object, and it sits in different places for different observers — treating the mirror as a window rather than a reflecting surface.
'There is no image unless the object is directly in front of the mirror.'
Confusing real and virtual images: believing a virtual image can be caught on a screen, that a real image is 'inside' the lens/mirror, or that a plane-mirror image is real.
Drawing reasoning that silently violates the law of reflection, and measuring angles loosely from the surface/lens instead of from the normal/axis.
Confusing plane mirrors with curved/spherical mirrors, and believing a bigger mirror makes a bigger image.

activities.title: Catch it, then lose it: the real image on a screen
steps: Set up a real converging lens, a bright object (e.g. a window or a lit arrow), and a screen on an optical bench or table.
Before moving anything, predict out loud: what will appear on the screen? Will it be upright or inverted, bigger or smaller?
Slide the screen until a sharp image forms; record whether it is inverted and how its size compares to the object.
Predict what happens if the lens is removed, then remove it and observe that the sharp image vanishes, leaving only a general patch of light on the screen (no image stays, and nothing flips upright).
Predict what happens if you cover half the lens with card, then do it and observe that the WHOLE image survives, just dimmer.
activities.insight: A real image forms where light rays actually converge, so it can be caught on a screen and is inverted; the lens is what makes the rays converge, and every part of the lens helps form the whole image.

activities.title: Construct the converging-lens diagram
steps: On paper, draw the optical axis and mark the lens, the focal point F, and 2F on both sides first.
Draw an object arrow standing on the axis beyond 2F.

From the top of the object draw the three principal rays: (1) parallel to the axis, then refracting through the far focal point; (2) straight through the centre of the lens, undeviated; (3) through the near focal point, emerging parallel to the axis.
Mark the image where the refracted rays actually cross, draw the image arrow, and state whether it is real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished.

Repeat for an object between F and 2F, and for an object inside F — for the inside-F case the two reliable rays (parallel ray and centre ray) no longer cross on the far side, so extend them back as dashed lines to find the virtual image.
activities.insight: Where real refracted rays cross is a real, inverted image; for a converging lens with the object inside F the emerging rays diverge and must be traced back, and the crossing of those dashed extensions marks a virtual, upright, magnified image — all from one standard construction.

activities.title: Plane-mirror virtual image and 'where must the eye be?'
steps: Draw a plane mirror and an object point in front of it.
Draw two rays from the object point to the mirror and reflect each so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the NORMAL (the line perpendicular to the mirror).
Extend the two reflected rays BACKWARDS as dashed lines behind the mirror; mark the virtual image where they meet.
Check that the image is upright, same-size, laterally inverted (left and right appear swapped), and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Mark an eye position and show that it sees the image by looking along the reflected rays; move the eye and discuss whether the image still exists and where it appears to be.
Use the question 'where would the eye have to be to see this?' and test a counterfactual, e.g. does stepping back change how much of yourself you can see in the mirror?
activities.insight: A plane-mirror image is virtual (formed by dashed back-extensions, cannot be caught on a screen), upright, same-size, laterally inverted, and equal distance behind; it exists whether or not you look straight at it, and the diagram — not a memorised distance rule — answers questions about what you can see.

activities.title: One construction, three devices
steps: Lay out three object positions: beyond 2F, between F and 2F, and inside F.
For each, use the completed lens diagram to read off real/virtual, orientation, and size.
Match each case to its device: beyond 2F → camera (real, inverted, diminished); between F and 2F → projector (real, inverted, magnified); inside F → magnifying glass (virtual, upright, magnified).
Explain a real device using the diagram: why a camera's image on the sensor is inverted, and why a magnifying glass must be held close to the object.
Answer transfer questions, e.g. if the object moves from just outside F to just inside F, describe how the image changes.
activities.insight: The three familiar optical devices are not separate facts to memorise but different regions of a single object-distance sweep through one construction.

activities.title: Manipulable optical-bench model (optional dynamic scaffold)
steps: Using a draggable optical-bench model, drag the object arrow along the axis and watch the three principal rays redraw live and meet at the image (for a virtual image, it is their dashed backward extensions that meet).
Toggle a screen to try to catch the image, and notice that a real image lands on the screen while a virtual one refuses to project.
Use a shutter to cover half the lens and observe the image dim but stay whole; use a control to remove the lens and watch the image vanish.
Switch to plane-mirror mode and drag an eye position to test 'can I see the image from here?'.

Use a 'you draw the rays' mode where you place the principal rays yourself and the model checks them, then sweep the object inward towards F and watch the inverted real image grow larger and move farther from the lens as the object nears F, then become a large upright virtual image once the object is inside F.
activities.insight: Seeing the construction redraw as the object moves makes the covariation between object position and image properties concrete, and the built-in experiments make the key refutations immediate.

checkQuestion: Here is a ray diagram of a converging lens with an object drawn well beyond the focal point. Two rays leave the top of the object, pass through the lens, and CROSS on the far side. Point to where the image forms and tell me three things about it — is it real or virtual, upright or inverted, bigger or smaller — and how the diagram tells you each one. Then take this second lens diagram, where I've only drawn the object and the lens, and YOU draw the two rays and mark the image.
checkAnswer: The image is where the refracted rays actually cross (on the opposite side of the lens from the object): it is REAL (rays genuinely meet there, so it could be caught on a screen), INVERTED (the crossed rays put the image top below the axis), and — for an object beyond 2F — DIMINISHED. In the second diagram the child draws the parallel ray (refracting through the far focal point) and the ray straight through the lens centre, and marks the image where they cross.
